rv.q: Rylance, often playing directly to the audience, has enjoyable moments of excruciating Father-dancing at the wedding and, as the English farce tradition demands, is more than once reduced to his white Y-fronts and vest.
As a show, it’s as big of heart as it’s loud of mouth and, ultimately, just an awful lot of fun.
Overall then, a refresh which speaks to multiculturalism, loyalty, traditions, and in a world which daily gives us cause to question established truth, a healthy and appropriate dose of cynicism.
The Nigerian-Jamaican setting suits Molière nicely, and Raymond’s production will only grow in strength as the run continues.
While the project is flawed, she and Rylance make this worth seeing.
This is a witty and impressive adaptation of the classic comedy that gives new life to a story centuries old.
This new version blasts the cobwebs from Moli re's wig and electrifies the original narrative with new relevance.
Tartuffe (Remixed) is energetic, clever and hilarious, while still finding room to explore family, faith and tradition.
Raymond’s experience adapting 15 Shakespeare plays and deftness in verse pulses through effortlessly: one of the production’s greatest strengths.
The whole production feels full of colour, movement and personality.
A riotous night out is to be had here, whether you know the original text or not.
It’s an energetic, inventive and thoroughly entertaining night at the theatre.
Mark Rylance is the major drawcard in this production, and he is very entertaining as the ingratiating vicar whose true colours begin to be revealed, especially in the second half of the play.

cn.t: Raymond's vibrant Nigerian-Jamaican adaptation brings fresh energy and sharp rhyming couplets to Molière's classic, with Rylance's grotesque Pastor Blake leading an entertaining farce that mostly succeeds despite occasionally losing political bite.
